Q: Generating points and discarding the first few points with Python A:

Problem Explanation

There are two main issues in your code:

  1. Incorrect loop range
    You initialized an array with 1000 rows:
x = np.zeros((1000, 2))

but you are looping over:

for i in range(1001):

This causes an index out-of-bounds error. The correct range is range(1000).

  1. Invalid assignment
x = 'int + [i , i] / 2'

This line assigns a string to x instead of numeric values. You need to assign values to a specific row of the array.

Correct Way to Build the Array

If you want 1000 points where each point is (i/2, i/2):

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.zeros((1000, 2))

for i in range(1000):
    x[i] = [i / 2, i / 2]

Plotting with plt.scatter()

The plt.scatter() function expects separate x and y arrays:

plt.scatter(x[:, 0], x[:, 1])
plt.xlabel("X")
plt.ylabel("Y")
plt.show()

Better NumPy Solution (No Loop)

You can generate the same result more efficiently using NumPy vectorization:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Generate an array of 1000 points
i = np.arange(1000)
# Create a (N, 2) array with x and y coordinates
x = np.column_stack((i / 2, i / 2))

# Plot the points using scatter plot
plt.scatter(x[:, 0], x[:, 1])
plt.show()

Summary

  • Create a (N, 2) NumPy array where each row represents a point.
  • Pass each column separately to plt.scatter().
  • Prefer NumPy vectorization over loops when possible.

Q: Difference between 'cls' and 'self' in Python classes? A:

The name of the first parameter of a class method can be any (self, this, cls, whatever ..) the important thing is how you use the method itself

In most cases you want to work with the object of the instance where each instance keep its own member variables like firstname, lastname, etc... Then the convention is calling the first parameter "self"

But if you use the decorator @classmethod (it is not just a "decorator"!) python passes a different object to the method, affecting none of the instance member variables but class variables for all instances. In that cases the convention is to use "cls"

There is another possibility using the decorator @staticmethod where python then simply does not pass any object in the first parameter

This code shows that the provided example is actually working with different type of member variables when using @classmethod and therefore not correct (unless you want to have an extra first name and last name for all the persons)

class Person:
    def __init__(self, firstname, lastname):
        self.firstname = firstname
        self.lastname = lastname

    @classmethod
    def from_fullname(cls, fullname):
        cls.firstname, cls.lastname = fullname.split(' ', 1)

    @classmethod
    def allPersonNames (cls):
        return f"{cls.firstname} & {cls.lastname}"

    def __str__ (self):
        return f"1st [{self.firstname}] 2nd:[{self.lastname}] (class names: {self.allPersonNames()})"

persona1 = Person("Patrice", "Lumumba")
persona2 = Person("Shireen", "")

# setting class names for all!
persona2.from_fullname ("Victor Jara")

print (persona1)
print (persona2)

which gives the output

1st [Patrice] 2nd:[Lumumba] (class names: Victor & Jara)
1st [Shireen] 2nd:[] (class names: Victor & Jara)

showing that an instance is working with 4 member variables (2 instance + 2 class)

Notice also that even if we call self.allPersonNames() using the instance object 'self' python passes only the class to the method because of the decorator @classmethod

Q: Firebase.auth error with 400 bad request A:

It is not clear what you are doing, but it appears that you are using the API incorrectly and insecurely. The plain user object contains a refresh token that is indefinite. Passing it around via URL is a really bad idea.

First don't rely on internal implementations, it is subject to change. To get the user's information on your backend, the right way to do it, is to get the user's ID token using officially supported API, eg user.getIdToken(), then pass it to your server.

On your server, you verify it via the Firebase Admin SDK: admin.auth().verifyIdToken(idToken). Then you know this is a real authenticated user. If you need the full user info, you can then look it up using the decoded user id in the token: admin.auth().getUser(decodedIdToken.sub).

Q: java.sql.SQLException: ORA-28040: No matching authentication protocol DSRA0010E: SQL State = 99999, Error Code = 28,040 A:

You didn't post any configuration information or server logs, so, assuming the old Oracle connection URL was working prior to you changing it, one common cause of this problem is changing the connection URL to move from an Oracle 11 instance (or earlier) to an Oracle 12 instance without properly updating the classpath of the WebSphere JDBC Provider to use at least the ojdbc6.jar.

Q: Identify Column Clicked in Gtk.Treeview A:

I'm not sure but TreeViewColumn can be indenpenden object and may not know number it has in Treeview.

But inIn Python you can always assign own variables

column.my_number = i

and later you can get this column.my_number in function

print(column.my_number)

By the way:

Documentation shows that you can use

column.set_data("my_number", i)
i = column.get_data("my_number")

but it raises error and it suggests to use normal

column.my_number = i
i = column.my_number

You don't have to send column to column_id(...) because you already get it in widget

print(widget.my_number)

But maybe you should send number instead of column

column.connect('clicked', self.column_id, i)

def column_id(self, widget, number):

It seems you can also ask treeview for index of column/widget

index = self.treeview.get_columns().index(widget)

And to get all values in this column

values = [row[index] for row in self.software_liststore]
#values = [row[widget.my_nymber] for row in self.software_liststore]

Full code used for tests:

import gi

gi.require_version("Gtk", "3.0")
from gi.repository import Gtk

software_list = [("Firefox", 2002, "C++"), ("Eclipse", 2004, "Java")]


class TreeViewFilterWindow(Gtk.Window):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.set_default_size(500, 200)

        self.grid = Gtk.Grid()
        self.grid.set_column_homogeneous(True)
        self.grid.set_row_homogeneous(True)
        self.add(self.grid)

        self.software_liststore = Gtk.ListStore(str, int, str)
        for software_ref in software_list:
            self.software_liststore.append(list(software_ref))

        self.current_filter_language = None

        self.treeview = Gtk.TreeView(model=self.software_liststore)
        self.treeview.set_headers_clickable(True)  # Probably not necessary

        for i, column_title in enumerate(["SW", "Year", "Language"]):
            renderer = Gtk.CellRendererText()
            column = Gtk.TreeViewColumn(column_title, renderer, text=i)

            # This allows the column to be clicked, but how do I identify, whick column I clicked?
            column.set_sort_column_id(True)
            column.set_clickable(True)
            column.connect("clicked", self.column_id)
            column.my_number = i
            # column.set_data("column-id", i)  # it suggests to set `column.column_id = i`

            self.treeview.append_column(column)

        ########
        self.scrollable_treelist = Gtk.ScrolledWindow()
        self.grid.attach(self.scrollable_treelist, 0, 0, 8, 10)
        self.scrollable_treelist.add(self.treeview)
        self.show_all()

    def column_id(self, widget):
        print("widget:", widget)

        print("title :", widget.get_title())
        print("my_number:", widget.my_number)
        # print("column-id:", widget.get_data("column-id"))  # it suggests to get `i = widget.column_id`

        index = self.treeview.get_columns().index(widget)
        print("index    :", index)

        values = [row[index] for row in self.software_liststore]
        print("values (index)    :", values)

        values = [row[widget.my_number] for row in self.software_liststore]
        print("values (my_number):", values)

        print("---")


win = TreeViewFilterWindow()
win.connect("destroy", Gtk.main_quit)
win.show_all()
Gtk.main()

Q: How to re-arrange / swizzle element pairs in a flat array using numpy? A:

Yes. A common NumPy approach is to reshape the array into (-1, 3), reorder the columns, then flatten it back:

arr = np.array([x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2, ...])  
  
result = arr.reshape(-1, 3)[:, [0, 2, 1]].ravel()

That converts:

[x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2]

into:

[x1, z1, y1, x2, z2, y2]

Keep in mind that changing the element order requires moving data around, so NumPy will generally need to create a new array for the result. The reshape itself is usually just a view, but the column reordering step isn't.
